chunk_findings.detail: `bug_tag` only validates `add_l` against reserved prefixes, and `set_tags` only validates the requested target list. A reserved `wave:*` tag that already exists on the bug can therefore be removed by hand: given a bug whose tags are `["wave:foo"]`, calling `bug_tag(repo, "B1", add="security", remove="wave:foo")` passes the `_refusal(add_l)` check, `GS.adjust` produces `["security"]`, and `_apply` appends `bug.tagged`, losing the scheduler-derived tag. Likewise, `set_tags(repo, "B1", ["security"])` succeeds and removes `wave:foo`, while `set_tags(repo, "B1", ["wave:foo", "security"])` is refused for containing a reserved tag, leaving no way to set non-reserved tags while preserving reserved `wave:*` tags. This contradicts the stated invariant that `wave:*` is reserved and never hand-edited.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/bug_tags.py:76

chunk_findings.detail: The new `bug tag` command is declared as an MCP mode of `ddflow_bug_fixed` (`via=("ddflow_bug_fixed", "tag")`) and contributes `add`/`remove` parameters to that tool, but it does not declare the `tag` boolean mode parameter that `_tagging()` in `ddflow/surfaces/tools/_common.py` reads. The existing alternate mode on the same tool has an explicit `Param("reopen", type="boolean", mcp_only=True)`; by contrast, `_tagging()` will always see `a.get("tag", False)` as false for MCP calls because no `tag` parameter is exposed. Thus an MCP client cannot invoke tag mode on `ddflow_bug_fixed`; a call such as `ddflow_bug_fixed(id="Bsecbug-...", add="security")` will not add the tag and will instead fall through to the tool's normal fixed/close behavior (or be rejected if `tag` is passed but not declared), breaking the intended CLI/MCP parity.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/records.py (new `bug tag` `Command`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test does not actually exercise an old log: it creates `B1` through the new `bug found` command and then reads `.tags`. It never builds a pre-change event log, removes a `tags` field from a `bug.found` event, or otherwise forces the fold through the missing-tags/upcaster/default path. If the fold lacks the required default for old logs, this test can still pass because the current CLI path may write a tags field (or the model may already have a default), so the stated old-log replay regression is not covered.

chunk_findings.detail: `set_tags` validates reserved tags against the `held` snapshot loaded by `_load`, but the tags actually written are produced by `_apply` from a freshly loaded `now` state, with no revalidation or atomic check. Given a bug whose tags are initially `["wave:foo"]`, a call `set_tags(repo, "B1", ["wave:foo"], agent=...)` passes the reserved check because `wave:foo` is in `held`. If the scheduler then appends an event removing `wave:foo` before `_apply` reloads the bug, `_apply` sees `now` without `wave:foo`, so `reserved(now)` is empty and the comprehension appends `wave:foo` from `tags` as an ordinary tag. The resulting `bug.tagged` event therefore adds a reserved `wave:*` tag by hand, violating the “only the scheduler writes wave tags” invariant.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/bug_tags.py:set_tags

chunk_findings.detail: The test is named for a `get_tags`/`set_tags` round trip and for removing `security`, but it never asserts the tag state before or after `set_tags` or `--remove security`. If `BT.get_tags` is broken and returns `[]` (or omits `security`) while `BT.set_tags` is a no-op that still returns `ok`, the existing `security` tag can still be removed by the later CLI call, leaving `wave:2`, so the final assertion `_tags(repo, "B1") == ["wave:2"]` passes. Equally, if the manual `bug.tagged` event or fold drops `security` but preserves `wave:2`, the `--remove security` call becomes a no-op and the same final assertion passes. Thus the test can pass even when the get/set tags pair—the API intended for the label engine—is wrong; it should assert that `security` is present before removal and that the expected tags are present after the set/remove operations.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_bug_tags.py:test_set_get_round_trips_and_a_re_report_does_not_undo_a_removal

chunk_findings.detail: The reserved-`wave:*` check in `set_tags` is performed against a state read outside the log lock (`_load(...)` then `held = get_tags(st, bug)`), while the actual decision and event append happen later under `log.transaction()` in `_apply`. Given a bug currently holding `wave:foo`, one caller can call `set_tags(repo, bug, ["wave:foo", "security"])`, read `held = ["wave:foo"]`, and pass the stale check; before that caller enters `_apply`, another writer/scheduler can remove `wave:foo`. Inside `_apply`, the folded current state no longer holds `wave:foo`, but the captured `tags` list still contains it, and the lambda includes it because it is not in `reserved(now)`. The result is a new `bug.tagged` event restoring/creating a derived `wave:*` tag, violating the “wave:* stays reserved / only scheduler writes them” rule and the code comment that the decision is made under the lock.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/bug_tags.py:set_tags

chunk_findings.detail: `set_tags` does not round-trip an existing tag list when a reserved tag is not already first. If the bug’s stored tags are `["security", "wave:foo"]`, then `get_tags` returns that list and calling `set_tags(repo, bug, ["security", "wave:foo"])` passes the reserved check. The lambda in `_apply` returns `[*reserved(now), *(t for t in tags if t not in reserved(now))]`, which becomes `["wave:foo", "security"]`. Because `_apply` compares lists, it treats this as a change (`was != tags`) and appends a spurious `bug.tagged` event even though the caller asked to set the tags back to the value just read.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge/bug_tags.py:set_tags

chunk_findings.detail: The new tag action is declared with `tag`, `add`, and `remove` all marked `mcp_only=True`. In this surface declaration, `mcp_only` hides the parameter from the CLI (as with `regression_tests`), so the CLI cannot pass the tag mutation parameters. Consequently the intended CLI form `ddflow bug tag BUG --add x --remove y` (or the equivalent `--tag --add/--remove` form on the existing bug tool) is not exposed/accepted by the declared CLI surface; only the MCP tool can perform the tag action. This violates the stated intent that `ddflow bug tag BUG --add x --remove y` work on an existing bug.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/declared/records.py:ddflow_bug_fixed params

chunk_findings.detail: The new tag mode is declared as an MCP mode of `ddflow_bug_fixed` (`via=("ddflow_bug_fixed", "tag")`) and `_tagging` is added to detect that mode, but nothing in the changed files calls `_tagging` or otherwise routes `ddflow_bug_fixed` to `_bug_tag`; `_bug_tag` is reached only from the CLI lambda in `ddflow/surfaces/declared/records.py`. Given an MCP call such as `ddflow_bug_fixed({"id": "B1", "tag": true, "add": "security"})`, the tool will follow the existing `ddflow_bug_fixed` path (or fail its existing validation) instead of calling `api.knowledge.bug_tags.bug_tag`, so the tag is not added via MCP. This breaks the stated MCP parity and leaves the strict mode checker dead.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/tools/_common.py:_tagging

chunk_findings.detail: The added MCP test is intended to cover `bug found --tags` over MCP, but it never checks the tag state after the `ddflow_bug_found` call. It only asserts exit `0`, then calls `ddflow_bug_fixed(..., add="x", remove="security")` and finally asserts `_tags(repo, "B1") == ["x"]`. If the MCP `ddflow_bug_found` handler ignores or does not wire the `tags` argument, the bug is created with no tags; the subsequent `remove="security"` is a no-op on an absent tag, `add="x"` still produces `["x"]`, and the test passes. Thus this test does not actually regress the required `bug found --tags` MCP parity.
